title: Which research direction, and which approach within it?
question: To find why food-bank sites run out of stock, should the study mine records, ask people, or simulate, and which approach should it use?
summary: A fictional benchmark, for demonstration only. Three research directions with nine approaches between them, each tried three times on five invented food-bank concepts whose cause is known. Two identical copies of one approach show how far chance alone moves a result.

alternatives.label: Regression on inventory logs
alternatives.content: Fit a regression of weekly stock-outs on the public inventory logs and report the strongest predictor.

alternatives.label: Regression on inventory logs (rerun)
alternatives.content: Fit a regression of weekly stock-outs on the public inventory logs and report the strongest predictor.

alternatives.label: Seasonal time series
alternatives.content: Model the weekly stock-out series with seasonality and trend, then report what the residuals point to.

alternatives.label: Text mining of case reports
alternatives.content: Read the free-text incident reports, cluster the stated reasons for each stock-out, and report the largest cluster.

alternatives.label: Short survey of coordinators
alternatives.content: Send a ten-question survey to every site coordinator and report the cause most often ranked first.

alternatives.label: Structured interviews
alternatives.content: Interview six coordinators with the same fixed question list and report the cause they converge on.

alternatives.label: Open interviews
alternatives.content: Interview six coordinators with open prompts only and report the cause that comes up unprompted.

alternatives.label: Agent-based simulation
alternatives.content: Build an agent-based model of donors, volunteers and clients, vary one factor at a time, and report which change removes the most stock-outs.

alternatives.label: Queueing model
alternatives.content: Model each site as a queue with arrivals and service rates and report the bottleneck.

cases.label: Seasonal demand swings
cases.description: Fictional network where the planted cause of stock-outs is demand that peaks every winter.

cases.label: Supplier reliability
cases.description: Fictional network where the planted cause is one supplier that delivers late.

cases.label: Donation timing
cases.description: Fictional network where the planted cause is drop-offs bunched at the start of the week.

cases.label: Volunteer turnover
cases.description: Fictional network where the planted cause is a weekend crew that keeps changing; nobody records who works.

cases.label: Storage capacity
cases.description: Fictional network where the planted cause is a cold room that is too small; usage is not logged.

metrics.label: Recovered the planted cause
metrics.description: Whether the run's conclusion names the cause planted in the concept's data.

metrics.label: Evidence quality
metrics.description: A blind reviewer's score for how well the evidence supports the conclusion.

metrics.label: Stated confidence
metrics.description: The confidence the run stated; neither level is better.

decision_rule: Carry forward the direction with the highest pooled recovery, if it reaches 60% of valid runs and none of the five concepts falls below 50% for it. Within that direction, choose the approach with the highest recovery, if it leads the next one by more than the gap between the two identical copies; otherwise carry the whole direction forward.
